summary: Gives an overview of the InfiniBand architecture, a high-speed channel-based interconnect between systems and devices. It then describes requirements and guidelines for transmitting IP over InfiniBand, for both IPv4 and IPv6. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: InfiniBand is a fast switched network for connecting computers and storage inside a data centre. RFC 4392 explains how ordinary IP traffic is carried over it, including how addresses are assigned, how multicast groups are joined, and why the design uses the connectionless service that every InfiniBand device supports.

what is an infiniband subnet manager
subtitle: A tour of InfiniBand and the ground rules for running IPv4 and IPv6 over it.

tldr.problem: InfiniBand is a switched fabric with its own addressing, its own multicast model and several different transfer services, so running ordinary IP over it needs a set of rules about which service to use and how IP addresses map onto fabric addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes the InfiniBand architecture, then explains that IP is carried over the Unreliable Datagram service, that each IP subnet is an overlay joined to a broadcast group managed by the subnet manager, and that the link-layer address is a GID plus a queue pair number.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational overview. The encapsulation and the address resolution mechanism are specified in RFC 4391, and DHCP over InfiniBand in RFC 4390.

today: RFC 4392 is an Informational document from April 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives an overview of the InfiniBand architecture and the requirements and guidelines for transmitting IP over it; the encapsulation of IP over InfiniBand and the address resolution mechanism are covered in RFC 4391, and DHCP over InfiniBand in RFC 4390.

sections.title: What InfiniBand Is
sections.content:
The InfiniBand Trade Association was formed to develop an I/O specification for a channel based, switched fabric technology, aimed at the scalability, reliability, availability and performance needs of servers in data centres. The InfiniBand Architecture defines a System Area Network for connecting multiple independent processor platforms, I/O platforms and I/O devices, supporting both I/O and inter-processor communications for one or more computer systems.

An InfiniBand SAN consists of processor nodes and I/O units connected through a fabric of cascaded switches and InfiniBand routers, the routers being the components that connect InfiniBand subnets. I/O units range from a single application-specific integrated circuit device such as a LAN adapter up to a large, memory-rich RAID subsystem. A network may be subdivided into subnets interconnected by routers; these are InfiniBand routers and InfiniBand subnets, not IP routers and IP subnets, and the document keeps the two sets of terms apart.

Each node or switch attaches to one or more switches, or directly to each other. Each unit interfaces with the link through channel adapters, and the architecture supports multiple channel adapters per unit, each providing one or more ports to the fabric, with each channel adapter appearing to the fabric as a node. The ports are the endpoints to which data is sent, and each port may carry multiple queue pairs that can be addressed directly from a remote peer. From the point of view of data transfer, the queue pair number is part of the address.

InfiniBand supports both connection-oriented and datagram service between ports. The peers are identified by queue pair number and port identifier, with two exceptions: queue pair numbers are not used when packets are multicast, and not in the Raw Datagram mode.
sections.plainLanguage: InfiniBand is a switched network for the inside of a data centre. Servers and disks plug in through adapters called channel adapters, and those adapters connect to switches. The fabric has its own address system and its own idea of a queue, which is why IP needs to be mapped onto it.

sections.title: Addresses in the Fabric: GID and LID
sections.content:
A port in a data packet is identified by a Local Identifier, and optionally by a Global Identifier. The GID is needed only when communicating across an InfiniBand subnet, though it may always be included. The GID is 128 bits long and is formed by the concatenation of a 64-bit InfiniBand subnet prefix and a 64-bit EUI-64-compliant portion, which is itself called the Global Unique Identifier. The LID is a 16-bit value assigned when the port becomes active. The GUID is the only persistent identifier of a port, but it cannot be used as an address in a packet, because if the prefix is modified the GID may change. The subnet manager may try to keep LID values constant across reboots, but that is not a requirement.

Assignment of the GID and the LID is done by the subnet manager. Every InfiniBand subnet has at least one subnet manager component, which assigns the LIDs and GIDs and programs the switches so they route packets between destinations. The subnet manager and the related subnet administrator are the central repository of everything needed to set up the fabric.

InfiniBand routers route packets between subnets based on GIDs, so within a subnet a packet may or may not carry a GID, while across subnets it must. A LID is always needed, since the destination within a subnet is determined by it.

The architecture borrows heavily from IPv6. Unicast GIDs have three scopes, exactly as in IPv6: link local, FE80/10, which the routers will not forward beyond the subnet; site local, FEC0/10, unique within a collection of subnets such as a data centre but not necessarily globally unique, which must not be forwarded outside the site; and global, which an InfiniBand router may use to route packets throughout an enterprise or the Internet. Multicast GIDs follow the IPv6 multicast format, FFxy:<112 bits>, where the nibble marked x holds four flag bits 000T and the nibble marked y holds the scope. The T bit distinguishes a permanently assigned, well-known GID from a transient group. The scope values run from link local at 2, through site local at 5 and organization-local at 8, to global at 0xE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each port has two identifiers. The LID is a short number that only means something inside one subnet and is handed out when the port comes up. The GID is a 128-bit address that is meaningful across the whole fabric, built from a subnet prefix and a permanent port identifier.

sections.title: How a Multicast Group Is Created and Joined
sections.content:
Multicast groups, identified by a Multicast Global Identifier, are managed by the subnet manager, which programs the switches so that packets reach every member that asked to receive them. InfiniBand distinguishes senders from receivers: all members of a group may transmit to it, but a port has to ask explicitly for packets addressed to the group to be forwarded to it.

A multicast group is created by sending a join request to the subnet manager, which records the group's GID and its characteristics. Those characteristics include the group path MTU, whether the group will be used for raw datagrams or unreliable datagrams, the service level, the partition key and the LID associated with the group, and they are fixed when the group is created. The manager assigns a multicast LID to the group and programs the switches to build the multicast tree.

A port joins a group with a join request and leaves with a leave message. As part of joining, the port receives the group characteristics, and the manager verifies that the requester can support the group MTU and reach the rest of the group members. For groups that span subnet boundaries the manager must work with the routers, and the MTU and the partition key have to match across subnets, because the partition key inserted into a packet is not modified by the switches or routers.

There is no create command. The first join request that sets the FullMember bit creates the group as a side effect, and the group is deleted as a side effect of the last FullMember leaving it. The creator of the group specifies the Q_Key, MTU, P_Key, service level, FlowLabel, TClass and scope, and may either ask for a suitable MGID to be created or name the MGID it wants; the multicast LID is assigned by the manager either way.

Each member is represented by a member record holding the MGID, the valid GID of the port, the Q_Key, the multicast LID, the MTU, the partition key, the service level, the scope and the JoinState. The JoinState bits describe what the port wants: FullMember means messages are routed to and from the port and the port counts as a member for group creation and deletion; NonMember means messages are routed to and from the port but the port is not counted as a member; SendOnlyNonMember means group messages are routed from the port but not to it. A port may set several bits, and the membership qualities are then the union of those states.
sections.plainLanguage: To receive a multicast group, a port asks the subnet manager to join it. The manager checks that the port can handle the group's settings, then programs the switches to copy the group's traffic to it. There is no separate create step: the first join creates the group.

sections.title: Which InfiniBand Service Carries IP
sections.content:
InfiniBand offers six ways of exchanging data between two endpoints, and IPoIB can be implemented over any, multiple, or all of them. The InfiniBand specification requires Unreliable Datagram mode to be supported by all InfiniBand nodes. Host channel adapters are specifically required to support Reliable Connected and Unreliable Connected modes, but the same is not true of target channel adapters, and support for the two Raw Datagram modes is entirely optional. The Raw Datagram mode uses a 16-bit checksum, against the better protection of a 32-bit checksum in the other modes.

Multicasting is a basic requirement of IP networks, and for simplicity, ease of implementation and integration with existing stacks it is desirable that the fabric support it. Multicasting in the switches is an optional feature of InfiniBand, and multicasting is possible only in Unreliable Datagram mode and the two Raw Datagram modes. The IPoIB specification therefore requires that multicast-capable InfiniBand fabrics be used to implement IPoIB subnets.

Only Unreliable Datagram mode is universal, supports multicast and provides a robust checksum, which makes it the obvious choice for IP over InfiniBand. Future documents might consider the connected modes, which offer a much larger MTU than Unreliable Datagram mode allows and benefit from the automatic path migration that the connected modes and the Reliable Datagram mode can support.

The IPoIB specification must not, and does not, require changes in IP and higher-layer protocols, nor does it mandate anything of IP stacks. The aim is that the changes be amenable to modularisation and incorporation into existing implementations at the same level as other media types. Each IP multicast group needs to be associated with a different InfiniBand multicast group as far as possible, to avoid duplicate packets in the fabric and unnecessary handling at the hosts, and a mapping process is defined in RFC 4391. Because the well-known InfiniBand MGIDs are reserved for the Raw Datagram mode, any mapping from IP multicast addresses must avoid them, so all IPoIB multicast GIDs always set the transient bit.
sections.plainLanguage: InfiniBand offers six kinds of transfer service. IP uses the connectionless one, because every device supports it, because it is the only reliable choice for multicast, and because it has the stronger checksum. The connected services are faster but not every device has them.

sections.title: Bringing Up an IPoIB Subnet
sections.content:
The IPoIB subnet is overlaid on the InfiniBand subnet, and is brought up in three steps. First, the all-IPoIB nodes multicast group, called the broadcast group, is created when the IP subnet is set up, either by the fabric administrator at the subnet manager or by the first IB_join. Creating a group requires values such as the partition key, Q_Key, service level, hop limit, flow identifier, traffic class and MTU, and these must be values that all potential members can work with. All unicast packets also need to use the partition key and Q_Key of the broadcast group.

Second, all IPoIB interfaces join the broadcast group. The broadcast group defines the span and the members of the IPoIB link, and joining it has the additional benefit of distributing the multicast group parameters to all members of the subnet. The join is a FullMember join, so if any of the ports or switches linking the port to the rest of the subnet cannot support the parameters, such as the path MTU or the partition key, the join request fails and the port does not become part of the IPoIB subnet. Third, the configuration parameters, such as the Q_Key and path MTU, are returned to the IPoIB node when it joins the broadcast group, and the partition key and the scope of the broadcast group have to be known before the join, though how they are determined is not specified.

Because the endpoints in a subnet must have compatible partition keys, an IP subnet has only one partition key associated with it, while an endpoint may have several. Since the partition key is unique in the subnet and is included in the MGID mappings from IP multicast addresses, every unique broadcast group MGID creates a separate abstract IPoIB link, and hence an IPoIB VLAN.

Multicast in an IPoIB subnet follows the same concepts as on any other medium, except that it requires interaction with the subnet manager. An IP multicast packet in Unreliable Datagram mode is laid out as the local routing header, the global routing header, the base transport header, the datagram extended transport header, the IP payload, the invariant checksum and the variant checksum. The global routing header carries the group GID and the local routing header carries the LID, and the switches route on the LID. A host that wants to send multicast attempts to join the relevant InfiniBand group first, because the fabric does not otherwise guarantee delivery. A pure sender may join as FullMember, in which case it also receives the group's traffic and keeps the group alive, or as SendOnlyNonMember, in which case it only sends and the group can be deleted once the full members have left. A receiver must join the group matching the IP address, and the group is created automatically if it does not exist.

IP routers learn of new IP groups through IGMP or MLD, but that is not enough here, because the router must also join the matching InfiniBand groups, and there is no promiscuous mode for listening to all packets. The router therefore asks the subnet manager to report every group creation and joins the reported groups, using the NonMember join mode so that its join does not stop the group being deleted when the real receivers leave. The service level used for traffic is chosen by each implementation's own policy; the InfiniBand specification leaves the usage and the mode of determination of the service level to the application, and no method or process for choosing it is defined by the IPoIB standards.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP subnet over InfiniBand is set up as a group that every interface joins. Joining hands out the settings the subnet needs, such as the maximum packet size and the partition key. If any switch along the way cannot handle those settings, the join fails and the interface stays out of the subnet.

sections.title: Address Resolution, Static Entries and DHCP
sections.content:
The encapsulation of IP packets in InfiniBand is described in RFC 4391. It specifies the use of an Ethertype value in all IPoIB communication packets, and the link-layer address is made up of the GID and the queue pair number. To let IPoIB subnets span multiple InfiniBand subnets, the specification uses the GID as part of the link-layer address. Because all packets in InfiniBand have to use the LID, address resolution has the extra step of resolving the destination GID, returned in response to an ARP or Neighbor Discovery request, to the LID. That phase of address resolution may also be used to determine other parameters needed for successful communication, such as the service level and the path rate.

All communication in the IPoIB subnet derives the Q_Key to use from the Q_Key specified in the broadcast group.

Static ARP entries and RARP server entries are based on invariant link addresses. In the case of IPoIB the link address includes the queue pair number, which might not be constant across reboots or even across network interface resets, so static ARP entries or RARP server entries will only work if the implementations using them can ensure that the queue pair number associated with an interface is invariant across reboots and resets.

DHCPv4 has a client identifier field of 16 octets, expected to hold the link-layer address, while the address in the case of IPoIB is 20 octets. To get around this, IPoIB specifies that the broadcast flag be used by the client when requesting an IP address.

On security, the document says it describes the InfiniBand architecture as relevant to IPoIB and restates issues specified in other documents, but specifies no requirements of its own, and introduces no security issues itself. IPoIB-related security issues are described in RFC 4391 and RFC 4390.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP address on InfiniBand resolves to a fabric address and a queue, and then to the short port number the switches actually route on. The queue number can change when a machine reboots, so hand-written address entries only work if the implementation keeps the queue number stable.

items.label: FullMember
items.desc: Messages destined for the group are routed to and from the port, and the port counts as a member for group creation and deletion.

items.label: NonMember
items.desc: Messages destined for the group are routed to and from the port, but the port is not considered a member for group creation or deletion.

items.label: SendOnlyNonMember
items.desc: Group messages are only routed from the port but not to it, and the port is not considered a member for group creation or deletion.
